paras: The banishment of Aaron P. Prioleau from Eutawville was the flight of Aaron P. Prioleau, a Black Republican politician, from his home in Eutawville, South Carolina, in April 1903, which he said he made to escape being lynched after a "pretended arrest." Prioleau described it in a letter asking Governor Heyward for protection, and the governor declined to act on what he called meagre facts.

Prioleau was contesting the election of Geo. S. Legare to Congress from the First District. He traced his danger to "the sad killing of my brother, John A. Fludd by citizens of said town," followed by prosecutions he called groundless, among them a concealed-weapons charge in Clarendon County that he denied. He also said a tenant charged in Fludd's killing, "backed up by the town and community of Eutawville," was holding his store and house by force.

"About the first of April last on the 8th of the same month," Prioleau wrote, he was forced to leave home "to save myself from being lynched after a pretended arrest." He said he was threatened with being "shot down" if seen in Eutawville, but he named no one, and no other account of the arrest was found.

Heyward replied that the letter was the only record before him and that "the facts are too meagre for me to take any executive action." He pointed Prioleau to the grand jury, a malicious-prosecution suit and local civil authorities, and asked for evidence that local officers had refused protection. No report of further action was found.

The Sumter Watchman and Southron printed the letter in full on June 24, 1903, under the headline "Prioleau Plays to the Galleries," describing "the excitable and lusty lunged Prioleau" telling of "his alleged wrongs." A week later it reported the governor's reply as "dignified and kindly in tone" and noted that Prioleau had "presented one side of the question." No Black newspaper account of the episode was found.

reader.title: Banishment of Aaron P. Prioleau from Eutawville
bases: Prioleau wrote that he was forced from his home in Eutawville under threat of lynching and of being shot if seen there, while his property was held by force (A3); the Watchman called him 'run out of his home town' (A4).
The only account of the flight and threats is Prioleau's own letter (A3); the governor's reply (A4) answers that letter and says it is the only record before him, so it is not an independent report.

accounts.label: Prioleau's letter to the governor
accounts.gist: Since his brother's killing his life and property had been in danger; after groundless prosecutions and a rent dispute he was forced to flee a threatened lynching after a 'pretended arrest' about April 1 or 8, and was threatened with being shot if he returned.

accounts.label: Governor's reply
accounts.gist: The governor said the only record before him was Prioleau's letter, that the facts were too meagre for action, and that the courts and local authorities offered redress.

accounts.label: Sumter editor
accounts.gist: The paper treated the complaint as political theater by an 'excitable' Republican leader and said he had presented one side.

framing.detail: The Watchman and Southron printed Prioleau's letter in full but under the headline 'Prioleau Plays to the Galleries', mocking him as 'excitable and lusty lunged' and his 'alleged wrongs' (A3), then called the governor's reply 'dignified and kindly' and said Prioleau got 'little satisfaction' (A4).

record_check.dossier: No charge is given for the April 'pretended arrest' that preceded his flight; the concealed-weapons charge (before Justice Richbourg in Clarendon County) is a separate earlier prosecution that Prioleau denied.
Unnamed; Prioleau blamed Eutawville 'citizens' and 'the town and community', including a tenant he says was charged in his brother's killing.
Not stated for Eutawville in the coverage; Berkeley and Clarendon are both named in connection with the prosecutions.
About April 1 or 8, 1903 (the letter's wording is ambiguous).
Single source: Prioleau's own letter; no independent report of the arrest or threats.
Two Watchman and Southron items (the letter, June 24, and the governor's reply, July 1); no Black-press coverage found.
